script.opening: "Hiya, I just need my omeprazole bumping up really — my indigestion’s been worse than usual the last few weeks and the normal dose isn’t cutting it. I’ve had a dodgy stomach for years so it’s nothing new, just a bad patch. Can you put a stronger script through? I haven’t got time to come in, we’re short-staffed at the warehouse."

facts.text: If explored: dyspepsia that has CHANGED and become persistent over ~6 weeks DESPITE a PPI; ~5 kg unintentional weight loss; EARLY SATIETY (full after a few mouthfuls); and — on direct asking — BLACK, tarry stools once or twice (possible melaena/GI bleeding). These alarm features point to an urgent suspected cancer pathway referral, not a dose increase.
He takes ibuprofen most days for back pain, NOT on his record — a major risk for peptic ulcer/GI bleeding, compounding the picture. He hasn’t connected it. H. pylori never tested.

HIDDEN AGENDA — he is minimising to avoid coming in because of WORK (short-staffed, fears being seen as unreliable, possibly job insecurity), and there’s a quieter fear: his weight loss and the black stools have frightened him, but admitting it might mean tests, time off, and bad news he can’t afford. The "just bump the dose" is avoidance.

Black tarry stools suggest upper-GI bleeding — potentially from an ulcer (NSAID-driven) or a tumour — and is a red flag that, with weight loss and treatment-resistant dyspepsia, needs urgent assessment, not a remote prescription.

Officially: a stronger PPI prescription over the phone, no visit. What he needs: recognition of alarm features (weight loss, early satiety, melaena, PPI-refractory) requiring a suspected cancer pathway referral, stopping the NSAID, and a same-day in-person assessment of possible GI bleeding (pulse, blood pressure, abdomen, FBC and U&E) — with the work barrier addressed.

ice.ideas: It’s just a bad patch of his long-standing indigestion; a stronger PPI over the phone will fix it.
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — minimising to avoid coming in because of work pressure/job insecurity, plus a quieter fear that the weight loss and black stools mean something serious he can’t afford to face.
ice.expectations: A stronger omeprazole prescription, no appointment. What he actually needs: a suspected cancer pathway referral for alarm features, stopping the NSAID, and assessment for GI bleeding.

cues: Dyspepsia CHANGED + persistent despite PPI + weight loss + early satiety — alarm features, not a dose issue.
Black tarry stools on direct questioning — possible melaena/GI bleed; ask specifically, he won’t volunteer it.
Daily ibuprofen not on the record — the hidden ulcer risk; and "no time, short-staffed" — the work-driven avoidance.

checkpoints.text: Identifies the ALARM FEATURES in dyspepsia — unintentional weight loss, early satiety, persistent/treatment-resistant symptoms despite PPI, and possible MELAENA (black tarry stools) — and does NOT simply increase the PPI over the phone

Asks specifically about GI bleeding (melaena, haematemesis) — recognising the patient won’t volunteer it — and recognises black tarry stools as a red flag suggesting upper-GI bleeding needing an in-person assessment the SAME DAY (pulse, blood pressure, abdomen, urgent FBC and U&E) — not a phone plan

Acts on the NICE NG12 pathway: a suspected cancer pathway referral for oesophageal or stomach cancer (replacing urgent direct-access endoscopy since the 2025 amendment) for people aged 55 and over with weight loss and upper abdominal pain, reflux or dyspepsia — he meets it — AND, because he reports black stools, a same-day in-person assessment today (emergency admission if bleeding is ongoing); restates the threshold, tagged NICE NG12 — and does not just "test and treat" when alarm features are present

Identifies and STOPS the hidden NSAID driver: daily ibuprofen (not on record) markedly raises peptic-ulcer/bleeding risk; advises stopping it and records it, addresses the back pain differently (NICE NG59: exercise-based care, not paracetamol alone; no NSAIDs while an ulcer or bleed is possible), and has H. pylori tested at endoscopy (NICE CG184: breath and stool antigen tests need a 2-week PPI washout, and the PPI should continue with a possible bleed)

Assesses acuity: sees him in person the same day because of the melaena, and if there are signs of significant/active bleeding (ongoing melaena, dizziness, haematemesis, haemodynamic symptoms) escalates to same-day/emergency assessment rather than a routine suspected cancer pathway referral
Hears the work-driven avoidance and the quieter fear; does not take the "just bump the dose" request at face value; brings him to accept assessment by naming the seriousness without panic
Problem-solves the work barrier (a morning for endoscopy, fit note if needed) and addresses the fear honestly, so he engages rather than deflects

Safety-nets clearly: red flags for urgent/emergency care (more black stools, vomiting blood, dizziness/collapse → A&E/999), stops the NSAID, arranges a same-day in-person review (pulse, BP, FBC for anaemia, U&E) and the suspected cancer pathway referral with H. pylori tested at endoscopy, documents, and follows up

worked.txt: "I hear you want this done quickly over the phone — but I can’t just increase the omeprazole, and I need to be straight about why. Indigestion that’s changed, isn’t responding to the tablets, with weight dropping off and feeling full quickly — that’s a different situation from a bad patch, and a higher dose could mask something we need to see."

"One important thing I have to ask directly: have your stools been black and tarry, or sticky, at all? … Once or twice. Okay — thank you, that’s really important. Black stools can mean a little bleeding higher up in the stomach or gullet, and combined with the weight loss, that’s something we look at urgently, not over the phone."

"Are you taking anything for your back? … Ibuprofen most days. That’s a key piece — anti-inflammatories like that are a common cause of stomach ulcers and bleeding, and it’s not on your records. I’d like you to stop it from today, and we’ll sort your back a safer way."

"So the plan is a camera test of your stomach and gullet, on the urgent suspected cancer pathway — usually straight to the test — because of the weight loss and the changed symptoms; they’ll test for a stomach bug called H. pylori during it. And because of the black stools, I need to see you in person today — pulse, blood pressure, a feel of your tummy and a blood count — not in a few days. If you have any more black stools, vomit blood, or feel dizzy or faint, that becomes A&E today, not a wait."

"I know the warehouse is short-staffed and that’s real pressure — but this won’t wait, and a camera test is usually just one morning. I’ll give you a note if you need it. Your health has to come first here; being off sick beats being seriously unwell."

"To be clear on the danger signs: more black or tarry stools, vomiting blood or what looks like coffee grounds, feeling lightheaded, a racing heart — any of those, call 999 or go to A&E. Stop the ibuprofen, keep taking the omeprazole as before. I’ll arrange the endoscopy urgently and follow your results. You rang for a stronger tablet; what you need is a proper look, and I’m going to make that happen safely."

f.learning: Long-standing dyspepsia that has CHANGED and become persistent despite a PPI, with unintentional weight loss, early satiety and — critically, on direct questioning — melaena (black tarry stools), is a cluster of ALARM features that mandates an urgent suspected cancer pathway referral, not a phone PPI dose increase. NICE NG12: refer using a suspected cancer pathway referral for oesophageal or stomach cancer (this replaced urgent direct-access endoscopy in 2025) at 55 and over with weight loss and upper abdominal pain, reflux or dyspepsia; the black stools also mean an in-person assessment the same day (pulse, BP, FBC, U&E), with emergency admission if bleeding is active. "Test and treat" (H. pylori) and a 4-week full-dose PPI (NICE CG184) are for uncomplicated dyspepsia WITHOUT alarm features — not here; with a possible bleed, H. pylori is tested at endoscopy. Two things are easily missed: melaena (the patient won’t volunteer it — ask specifically), and a hidden NSAID driver (daily ibuprofen not on the record, a major peptic-ulcer/bleeding risk) which must be stopped, alongside H. pylori testing at endoscopy and an FBC; the back pain then needs an NG59 plan (exercise-based care; not paracetamol alone). The examinable hidden agenda is work-driven avoidance (short-staffed, job insecurity) plus a quieter fear of bad news he can’t afford; name the seriousness without panic, problem-solve the work barrier, stop the NSAID, and safety-net the GI-bleed red flags clearly.

knowledge.guideline: NICE CG184 (2014, updated 2019) — GORD and dyspepsia in adults · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · NICE CG141 (2012, updated 2016) — acute upper GI bleeding · NICE NG59 (2016, updated 2026) — low back pain
knowledge.summary: Dyspepsia that has changed and persists despite a PPI, with 5 kg weight loss, early satiety and black stools, in a 58-year-old on daily ibuprofen, needs same-day assessment for bleeding and a suspected cancer pathway referral (often straight to endoscopy) — not a bigger PPI dose over the phone.

points.t: NICE NG12, recommendations 1.2.1 and 1.2.7 (amended 2025): refer people using a suspected cancer pathway referral for oesophageal or stomach cancer if they have dysphagia, or are aged 55 and over with weight loss and any of upper abdominal pain, reflux or dyspepsia. This replaced the earlier urgent direct-access endoscopy route. Paul meets the second limb.

Black, tarry stools suggest upper GI bleeding — from an NSAID ulcer or a tumour. He needs to be seen in person today: pulse, blood pressure, abdomen, and an urgent FBC and U&E. Ongoing melaena, haematemesis, dizziness, collapse or a fast pulse means emergency admission. In hospital, NICE CG141 uses the Glasgow-Blatchford score at first assessment.

NICE CG184 manages uninvestigated dyspepsia without alarm features with lifestyle and medicine review, a 4-week full-dose PPI or H. pylori test and treat. That pathway does not apply once weight loss, bleeding or persistent symptoms despite a PPI appear.

Over-the-counter ibuprofen taken most days, not on his record, is a major cause of peptic ulcer and GI bleeding (BNF: NSAIDs carry a risk of serious GI adverse effects). Stop it today and record it. Ask every dyspeptic patient about bought medicines.
NICE CG184: breath or stool antigen testing needs a 2-week washout from PPIs. With a possible bleed, keep the PPI going and let the endoscopy team test for H. pylori at endoscopy.

points.h: The back pain still needs a plan
points.t: NICE NG59: do not offer paracetamol alone for low back pain; exercise-based care is central, and NSAIDs are not an option while an ulcer or bleed is possible. Offer a review for the back once the GI picture is clear.
Suspected cancer pathway (NG12) endoscopy is usually one morning. The NHS England Faster Diagnosis Standard (October 2023) aims for cancer to be diagnosed or ruled out within 28 days of referral.

Alarm-feature dyspepsia with possible upper GI bleeding, likely NSAID-related, cancer to be excluded — explained in plain language.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

ro.d: “Worse than usual” and “no time to come in” explored; the black stools drawn out by direct questioning.
Idea (a bad patch of old indigestion), concern (fear about the weight and black stools, and about work), expectation (a stronger PPI with no visit).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — minimising to avoid coming in because of work pressure/job insecurity, plus a quieter fear that the weight loss and black stools mean something serious he can’t afford to face — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello, is that Mr Mercer? It’s Dr Lee. Can I just confirm your date of birth, and that you can talk freely? … Thanks. I see you’re after more omeprazole — tell me what’s been happening.
model.why: Identity and privacy check, then an open question

model.text: My indigestion’s been worse the last few weeks and the normal dose isn’t touching it. I’ve had a dodgy stomach for years. Can you just put a stronger script through? I haven’t got time to come in — we’re short-staffed.
I hear you’re pushed for time, and I’ll be efficient. Before I change any tablets I need a few minutes to understand what’s different this time — then we’ll decide together. Okay?
model.why: Acknowledges his constraint and agrees an agenda without promising the prescription

model.text: Yeah, go on.
You say it’s worse — how is it different from your usual indigestion, and how long has it been like this?
model.why: Establishes a change in a long-standing symptom

model.text: About six weeks. It’s there all the time now, not just after food. And I get full after a few mouthfuls.
Has your weight changed without trying?
model.why: Screens for weight loss — a NICE NG12 criterion at 55 and over

model.text: About five kilos, yeah. Thought it was the job.
I need to ask you something directly, because people often don’t mention it. Have your stools been black, tarry or sticky at all? Or have you vomited blood, or anything like coffee grounds?
model.why: Asks specifically about melaena and haematemesis

model.text: …Black, once or twice. I didn’t think much of it. No sick.
Thank you — that’s really important. Right now, do you feel dizzy or faint when you stand, or is your heart racing? Any more black stools today?
model.why: Assesses acuity to decide between emergency and same-day care

model.text: No, I’m all right in myself. Not today.
And are you taking anything else — anything from the chemist, for pain or anything?
Ibuprofen for my back. Most days, if I’m honest.
That helps a lot. Can I ask what you’ve made of it all yourself — the weight and the black stools?
Honestly? It’s frightened me a bit. But if I come in it’s tests and time off, and they’re already on at us at work. I can’t afford to be the one who’s off.
That’s a lot to be carrying — worried about what it is, and worried about work at the same time. Thank you for being straight with me. Let me be straight back.
model.why: Names both the fear and the work pressure

model.text: What you’re describing isn’t a bad patch of the old indigestion. Pain that’s changed and isn’t responding, feeling full quickly, weight loss and black stools — that combination needs looking at properly. A stronger tablet could hide it.
model.why: Declines the dose increase and names the alarm features

model.text: Black stools can mean bleeding from the stomach — often an ulcer, and ibuprofen is a common cause. So I’d like you to stop the ibuprofen from today, and I need to see you in person today to check your pulse, blood pressure and tummy, and do a blood count.
model.why: Stops the NSAID and arranges same-day assessment for possible bleeding

model.text: Alongside that, I’m referring you on the urgent suspected cancer pathway, which usually means a quick camera test of your gullet and stomach — at your age, with weight loss and indigestion, that’s what national guidance says. It’s to find the cause, which is very often an ulcer that heals, not a verdict.
model.why: States the NICE NG12 criterion with honest balance

model.text: Right. That’s… a lot. But okay.
What would help you get here today? I can give you a time at the end of your shift if that’s easier — but it does need to be today.
model.why: Problem-solves the work barrier without negotiating on urgency

model.text: I could get there straight after my shift.

Good, I’ll book you in for then. The camera test is usually one morning. If you need time off, you can self-certify for a week, and I can give you a fit note if it’s longer. Keep taking the omeprazole as you are. The endoscopy team can test for the stomach bug H. pylori at the same time. And we’ll sort your back without ibuprofen once we know what’s going on.
model.why: Practical plan: time off, PPI, H. pylori and the back pain

model.text: Until I see you — if you pass more black stools, vomit blood or anything like coffee grounds, feel dizzy, faint or your heart races, call 999 or go straight to A&E. Don’t wait for me.
model.why: Clear emergency triggers for an upper GI bleed

model.text: Can you tell me back what we’ve agreed, so I know I’ve been clear?
No ibuprofen, keep the omeprazole, see you after my shift for bloods and a check, camera test in the next two weeks. And 999 if I bring up blood or feel faint.
Spot on. You did the right thing ringing. See you this afternoon.

social.t: A supervisor in a short-staffed warehouse fears being seen as unreliable. Offer a slot after his shift and explain how short the endoscopy is; this turns a refusal into attendance.
Smoking adds to ulcer and cancer risk. Note it and offer stop-smoking support at a later contact (NICE NG209, 2021) — not in the middle of a possible bleed.

legal.t: Employees self-certify for the first 7 days of sickness absence; a fit note is needed after that. A single endoscopy morning rarely needs one.
If he has sedation for endoscopy he must not drive home and needs someone to collect him.

professional.t: GMC Good practice in prescribing and managing medicines and devices (2021): prescribe remotely only when you have enough information to do so safely. Alarm features and possible bleeding mean he must be assessed in person.
Record over-the-counter ibuprofen on his notes so future prescribers see it; this is a patient-safety issue, not just good housekeeping.
Suspected cancer referrals and urgent blood results should be tracked; the doctor who refers owns the follow-up.

community.t: Guts UK and Macmillan Cancer Support for information; the community pharmacist for advice on safer over-the-counter pain relief; local stop-smoking service.

playbook.diagnosis: Be honest: “This isn’t your usual indigestion. With weight loss, feeling full quickly and black stools, I’m worried about bleeding in the stomach — often an ulcer from ibuprofen — and I need to rule out anything more serious with an urgent camera test.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Your stomach has been sending the same message for years. Now it’s sending a different one — and the black stools are like finding oil under the car. We don’t just top up the oil; we find the leak.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve been worried about this and about work at the same time — that’s hard. Getting seen today is the quickest way back to feeling in control.”
management.psychosocial: Offer a same-day slot after his shift; explain self-certification and fit notes; reassure that endoscopy is usually a single morning.
sharedPlan: Stop ibuprofen today; continue omeprazole; same-day face-to-face check with urgent FBC and U&E
NICE NG12: suspected cancer pathway referral for oesophageal or stomach cancer (55+ with weight loss and dyspepsia), often straight to endoscopy; H. pylori tested at endoscopy
Back pain managed without NSAIDs (NICE NG59); stop-smoking support later
safetyNet: More black stools, vomiting blood or coffee grounds, dizziness, faintness or racing heart → 999 or A&E
Follow-up of bloods and endoscopy result; confirm the hospital date arrives

pitfalls.intro: This telephone station is built to tempt a quick prescription. It is passed by asking two direct questions — about black stools and bought medicines — and failed by answering the request instead of the patient.

items.fail: Increasing the omeprazole over the phone as requested.
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” Weight loss with dyspepsia at 55 and over meets NICE NG12 for a suspected cancer pathway referral; a higher PPI dose masks the picture.
items.fix: Ask what has changed, find the alarm features, then explain why a stronger tablet is the wrong kindness.

items.fail: Never asking about black stools or vomiting blood.
items.why: Patients rarely volunteer melaena; missing it misses the most urgent part of the case.
items.fix: “I need to ask directly — have your stools been black, tarry or sticky?”

items.fail: Missing the over-the-counter ibuprofen because it is not on the record.
items.why: Unrecorded NSAIDs are a leading cause of ulcers and bleeding; stopping them is part of the treatment.
items.fix: “Anything from the chemist, for pain or anything else?” Then stop it and record it.

items.fail: Referring for endoscopy but leaving possible bleeding to wait two weeks.
items.why: Black stools need same-day assessment of pulse, blood pressure and Hb; an unstable patient needs emergency admission.
items.fix: Judge acuity on the call, then see him today and send the urgent referral.

items.fail: Arguing with him about work or telling him his job doesn’t matter.
items.why: Dismissing his real constraint loses him; examiners reward negotiation that keeps the clinical line.
items.fix: Tailor the time — after his shift — but not the urgency.

items.fail: A vague “ring back if it gets worse” close.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting is a standard failing feedback statement, and here it is dangerous.
items.fix: Name the 999 triggers — more black stools, vomiting blood, dizziness, racing heart — and use teach-back.

Ibuprofen for my back. Most days, if I’m honest.
That helps a lot. Can I ask what you’ve made of it all yourself — the weight and the black stools?
Honestly? It’s frightened me a bit. But if I come in it’s tests and time off, and they’re already on at us at work. I can’t afford to be the one who’s off.
That’s a lot to be carrying — worried about what it is, and worried about work at the same time. Thank you for being straight with me. Let me be straight back.
SCA_MODELS.why: Names both the fear and the work pressure

SCA_MODELS.text: What you’re describing isn’t a bad patch of the old indigestion. Pain that’s changed and isn’t responding, feeling full quickly, weight loss and black stools — that combination needs looking at properly. A stronger tablet could hide it.
SCA_MODELS.why: Declines the dose increase and names the alarm features

SCA_MODELS.text: Black stools can mean bleeding from the stomach — often an ulcer, and ibuprofen is a common cause. So I’d like you to stop the ibuprofen from today, and I need to see you in person today to check your pulse, blood pressure and tummy, and do a blood count.
SCA_MODELS.why: Stops the NSAID and arranges same-day assessment for possible bleeding

SCA_MODELS.text: Alongside that, I’m referring you on the urgent suspected cancer pathway, which usually means a quick camera test of your gullet and stomach — at your age, with weight loss and indigestion, that’s what national guidance says. It’s to find the cause, which is very often an ulcer that heals, not a verdict.
SCA_MODELS.why: States the NICE NG12 criterion with honest balance

SCA_MODELS.text: Right. That’s… a lot. But okay.
What would help you get here today? I can give you a time at the end of your shift if that’s easier — but it does need to be today.
SCA_MODELS.why: Problem-solves the work barrier without negotiating on urgency

SCA_MODELS.text: I could get there straight after my shift.

Good, I’ll book you in for then. The camera test is usually one morning. If you need time off, you can self-certify for a week, and I can give you a fit note if it’s longer. Keep taking the omeprazole as you are. The endoscopy team can test for the stomach bug H. pylori at the same time. And we’ll sort your back without ibuprofen once we know what’s going on.
SCA_MODELS.why: Practical plan: time off, PPI, H. pylori and the back pain

SCA_MODELS.text: Until I see you — if you pass more black stools, vomit blood or anything like coffee grounds, feel dizzy, faint or your heart races, call 999 or go straight to A&E. Don’t wait for me.
SCA_MODELS.why: Clear emergency triggers for an upper GI bleed

SCA_MODELS.text: Can you tell me back what we’ve agreed, so I know I’ve been clear?
No ibuprofen, keep the omeprazole, see you after my shift for bloods and a check, camera test in the next two weeks. And 999 if I bring up blood or feel faint.
Spot on. You did the right thing ringing. See you this afternoon.

SCA_STEM.name: Paul Mercer
SCA_STEM.recent: Warehouse supervisor. H. pylori never tested. No endoscopy on record. No recent FBC.
SCA_STEM.reason: Telephone request to increase his omeprazole — “indigestion worse than usual”.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE CG184 (2014, updated 2019) — GORD and dyspepsia in adults · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · NICE CG141 (2012, updated 2016) — acute upper GI bleeding · NICE NG59 (2016, updated 2026) — low back pain
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Dyspepsia that has changed and persists despite a PPI, with 5 kg weight loss, early satiety and black stools, in a 58-year-old on daily ibuprofen, needs same-day assessment for bleeding and a suspected cancer pathway referral (often straight to endoscopy) — not a bigger PPI dose over the phone.

points.t: NICE NG12, recommendations 1.2.1 and 1.2.7 (amended 2025): refer people using a suspected cancer pathway referral for oesophageal or stomach cancer if they have dysphagia, or are aged 55 and over with weight loss and any of upper abdominal pain, reflux or dyspepsia. This replaced the earlier urgent direct-access endoscopy route. Paul meets the second limb.

Black, tarry stools suggest upper GI bleeding — from an NSAID ulcer or a tumour. He needs to be seen in person today: pulse, blood pressure, abdomen, and an urgent FBC and U&E. Ongoing melaena, haematemesis, dizziness, collapse or a fast pulse means emergency admission. In hospital, NICE CG141 uses the Glasgow-Blatchford score at first assessment.

NICE CG184 manages uninvestigated dyspepsia without alarm features with lifestyle and medicine review, a 4-week full-dose PPI or H. pylori test and treat. That pathway does not apply once weight loss, bleeding or persistent symptoms despite a PPI appear.

Over-the-counter ibuprofen taken most days, not on his record, is a major cause of peptic ulcer and GI bleeding (BNF: NSAIDs carry a risk of serious GI adverse effects). Stop it today and record it. Ask every dyspeptic patient about bought medicines.
NICE CG184: breath or stool antigen testing needs a 2-week washout from PPIs. With a possible bleed, keep the PPI going and let the endoscopy team test for H. pylori at endoscopy.

points.h: The back pain still needs a plan
points.t: NICE NG59: do not offer paracetamol alone for low back pain; exercise-based care is central, and NSAIDs are not an option while an ulcer or bleed is possible. Offer a review for the back once the GI picture is clear.
Suspected cancer pathway (NG12) endoscopy is usually one morning. The NHS England Faster Diagnosis Standard (October 2023) aims for cancer to be diagnosed or ruled out within 28 days of referral.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Identity and privacy checked; open question on what has changed; did not issue the prescription before assessing.
Warehouse supervisor, short-staffed and worried about being seen as unreliable; smoker; back pain driving daily ibuprofen.
“Worse than usual” and “no time to come in” explored; the black stools drawn out by direct questioning.
Idea (a bad patch of old indigestion), concern (fear about the weight and black stools, and about work), expectation (a stronger PPI with no visit).
Same-day pulse, BP and abdominal examination; urgent FBC and U&E; suspected cancer pathway referral under NICE NG12, often straight to OGD, with H. pylori testing at endoscopy.
NSAID peptic ulcer with bleeding, gastric or oesophageal cancer, gastritis; persistent symptoms despite a PPI weighed against uncomplicated dyspepsia.
Asked about melaena, haematemesis, dizziness and palpitations to judge whether he needs an ambulance now or same-day review.
Alarm-feature dyspepsia with possible upper GI bleeding, likely NSAID-related, cancer to be excluded — explained in plain language.
Stops ibuprofen; same-day assessment; NICE NG12 suspected cancer pathway referral (55+ with weight loss and dyspepsia); PPI continued; no test-and-treat instead.
Back pain plan without NSAIDs; smoking noted with support offered later; ibuprofen added to the record.
999 triggers for bleeding, a timed same-day appointment, self-certification and fit note explained, teach-back.

social.t: A supervisor in a short-staffed warehouse fears being seen as unreliable. Offer a slot after his shift and explain how short the endoscopy is; this turns a refusal into attendance.
Smoking adds to ulcer and cancer risk. Note it and offer stop-smoking support at a later contact (NICE NG209, 2021) — not in the middle of a possible bleed.

legal.t: Employees self-certify for the first 7 days of sickness absence; a fit note is needed after that. A single endoscopy morning rarely needs one.
If he has sedation for endoscopy he must not drive home and needs someone to collect him.

professional.t: GMC Good practice in prescribing and managing medicines and devices (2021): prescribe remotely only when you have enough information to do so safely. Alarm features and possible bleeding mean he must be assessed in person.
Record over-the-counter ibuprofen on his notes so future prescribers see it; this is a patient-safety issue, not just good housekeeping.
Suspected cancer referrals and urgent blood results should be tracked; the doctor who refers owns the follow-up.

community.t: Guts UK and Macmillan Cancer Support for information; the community pharmacist for advice on safer over-the-counter pain relief; local stop-smoking service.

redFlags: Dyspepsia that has changed and persists despite a PPI; early satiety
About 5 kg unintended weight loss at 58
Black stools once or twice — ask about haematemesis, dizziness, palpitations and collapse now
psychosocial: Short-staffed warehouse; fears being seen as unreliable
Daily over-the-counter ibuprofen for back pain, not on his record
ice: Idea: “It’s just a bad patch of my usual indigestion”
Concern: frightened by the weight loss and black stools, and by time off work
Expectation: a stronger omeprazole script with no visit

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Be honest: “This isn’t your usual indigestion. With weight loss, feeling full quickly and black stools, I’m worried about bleeding in the stomach — often an ulcer from ibuprofen — and I need to rule out anything more serious with an urgent camera test.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Your stomach has been sending the same message for years. Now it’s sending a different one — and the black stools are like finding oil under the car. We don’t just top up the oil; we find the leak.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve been worried about this and about work at the same time — that’s hard. Getting seen today is the quickest way back to feeling in control.”
management.psychosocial: Offer a same-day slot after his shift; explain self-certification and fit notes; reassure that endoscopy is usually a single morning.
sharedPlan: Stop ibuprofen today; continue omeprazole; same-day face-to-face check with urgent FBC and U&E
NICE NG12: suspected cancer pathway referral for oesophageal or stomach cancer (55+ with weight loss and dyspepsia), often straight to endoscopy; H. pylori tested at endoscopy
Back pain managed without NSAIDs (NICE NG59); stop-smoking support later
safetyNet: More black stools, vomiting blood or coffee grounds, dizziness, faintness or racing heart → 999 or A&E
Follow-up of bloods and endoscopy result; confirm the hospital date arrives

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This telephone station is built to tempt a quick prescription. It is passed by asking two direct questions — about black stools and bought medicines — and failed by answering the request instead of the patient.

items.fail: Increasing the omeprazole over the phone as requested.
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” Weight loss with dyspepsia at 55 and over meets NICE NG12 for a suspected cancer pathway referral; a higher PPI dose masks the picture.
items.fix: Ask what has changed, find the alarm features, then explain why a stronger tablet is the wrong kindness.

items.fail: Never asking about black stools or vomiting blood.
items.why: Patients rarely volunteer melaena; missing it misses the most urgent part of the case.
items.fix: “I need to ask directly — have your stools been black, tarry or sticky?”

items.fail: Missing the over-the-counter ibuprofen because it is not on the record.
items.why: Unrecorded NSAIDs are a leading cause of ulcers and bleeding; stopping them is part of the treatment.
items.fix: “Anything from the chemist, for pain or anything else?” Then stop it and record it.

items.fail: Referring for endoscopy but leaving possible bleeding to wait two weeks.
items.why: Black stools need same-day assessment of pulse, blood pressure and Hb; an unstable patient needs emergency admission.
items.fix: Judge acuity on the call, then see him today and send the urgent referral.

items.fail: Arguing with him about work or telling him his job doesn’t matter.
items.why: Dismissing his real constraint loses him; examiners reward negotiation that keeps the clinical line.
items.fix: Tailor the time — after his shift — but not the urgency.

items.fail: A vague “ring back if it gets worse” close.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting is a standard failing feedback statement, and here it is dangerous.
items.fix: Name the 999 triggers — more black stools, vomiting blood, dizziness, racing heart — and use teach-back.
